analysis.one_liner: Lets lawsuits over warrantless wiretapping continue against the government instead of the phone companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2009 and never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2008 law gave telephone and internet companies legal immunity for helping the government's warrantless wiretapping program, which was killing lawsuits brought by Americans who believed their communications were swept up. This bill would have replaced the phone companies with the U.S. government as the defendant in those cases — but only after the secret FISA court reviewed the government's directives and found them lawful. Plaintiffs would also get limited rights to seek documents from the companies and could revive claims already thrown out under the 2008 immunity. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who sued telecom companies claiming their communications were swept into the warrantless surveillance program between 2001 and early 2007. If the bill passed, they would gain a defendant that can actually be sued — the United States, with sovereign immunity waived for these claims — a required review by the FISA court of whether the government's directives were legal, and the right to serve document requests on the companies even after claims against them are dismissed. Plaintiffs whose claims were dismissed under the 2008 immunity could refill them against the government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Surveillance plaintiffs suing over warrantless wiretapping

how_it_helps.text: Replaces telecom companies with the United States as defendant in covered civil actions once the Attorney General certifies the alleged assistance was done under a written presidential directive, so plaintiffs can still pursue the underlying claims rather than lose them outright.

Waives sovereign immunity for these substituted claims and deems claims timely filed against the government if they were timely filed against the provider, so plaintiffs would not lose their cases on technical grounds.

Requires the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court to determine whether the government's written directive to the company was lawful and whether the company acted in good faith, and lets plaintiffs and defendants appear before that court during the review.

Lets plaintiffs serve third-party discovery requests on the electronic communication service providers, with the companies' deposition answers and admissions binding on the government — a window into what actually happened even after the companies are dismissed.

Allows claims dismissed under the 2008 retroactive immunity (title VIII of the FISA Amendments Act) to be tolled and refilled against the United States, and provides an alternative path if the FISA court finds the immunity statute unconstitutional.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and ultimately taxpayers, would bear the liability and litigation costs for the surveillance program once substituted as defendant. The phone and internet companies keep their immunity from the 2008 law and their role in assisting the program would never be tested in open court. Plaintiffs would still face an uphill fight: if the secret FISA court finds the government's directives were lawful, their claims against the United States are dismissed.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not restore suits against the telecom companies themselves; every certified claim against them would be dismissed with final judgment, permanently locking in the immunity Congress granted in 2008, and accountability advocates argued any substitution bill conceded the companies' central win.

The Attorney General's certification can be submitted to the court in camera, ex parte, and under seal, with its contents never disclosed, and if the government claims national security harm, the FISA court may announce only whether its conditions were met without explaining why — so much of the review happens in secret.

If the FISA court finds the written directive was lawful, the claims against the United States would be dismissed, meaning plaintiffs could end up with no one left to sue and little discovery into the program itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a partial fix, not a clean one. Compared with doing nothing, it gave surveillance plaintiffs a live defendant, a court review of the government's directives, and some discovery rights that the 2008 immunity law denied them. But it accepted the telecom companies' permanent escape from liability and moved the accountability fight into a secret court where the government's certifications could stay hidden. An honest supporter would concede that the people most affected — customers whose communications were monitored — would never see the companies answer in open court, and would win only if a secret tribunal found the program illegal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it sat untouched until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the bill on April 23, 2009, with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse as its sole cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The full action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee markup or vote, and no floor action ever followed the referral.
The bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, leaving the 2008 telecom immunity law unchanged and the pending lawsuits unresolved by Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The telecommunications companies came out ahead: their immunity from the warrantless-wiretapping lawsuits under the 2008 law was never reopened, and no court ever had to review the government's directives under this bill's terms. The government likewise avoided the litigation risk of standing in as defendant.

sides.party_line_note: The only two senators involved were a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor of 58, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently dismissed all certified claims against the companies over their role in the warrantless surveillance program, locking in the immunity Congress gave them in 2008. Their interest in escaping liability runs against the surveillance plaintiffs', though the bill would have let plaintiffs take some sworn discovery from them even after dismissal.

industries.industry: U.S. intelligence community and executive branch
industries.note: The bill would have made the government, rather than private companies, the defendant for the surveillance program's legal consequences — a real accountability cost — while letting the Attorney General keep certifications secret and preserving immunity defenses in all other respects.
